Be careful who you trust with your private data!
  
The other days I found an AI evaluation role that looked like a good fit for my OSINT experience. It was about checking facts – I can do that, evaluating sources- I love doing that, and spotting claims an AI model had made up – it even sounded rewarding. So, I thought there was something to look into. And I did it the way I did everything in my life except for falling in love - before applying, I decided it was time for a fact-checking of my own.  
The hiring platform asks candidates to upload a CV and provide proof of their qualifications, such as a copies of their diploma. It also requests an ID check !!!! and a recorded interview. They say the interview recording, transcript, and scores might be shared with prospective clients and partners. Probably your CV, too, I might add. And the ID check at that incipient stage of recruiting was a veto all by itself. By then, there was a question on my mind: Who exactly would I be handing my data to?   
I checked the website, I found the brand name and a contact email. There was no mentioned company running it, no full legal name, registered address, or company registration number of the operator. I couldn’t establish who would sign the contract or pay me if I got the work done. So, I went on with my research.  I ran a WHOIS check. It showed that the website was registered on March 31, 2026, and that a privacy service is shielding the registrant’s identity. That left me with a relatively new domain, and another question mark involving the implied secrecy of the operator. It was a company using a privacy registrant in Holland for a website hosted on a USA server, that had behind it a person based in Lahore, Pakistan. Wellfound lists a person based in Lahore, Pakistan, as the website’s founder and also names a company in his work history. The same platform gives the hiring platform/company a size of 201–500 people, and some job listings carry a Chicago location tag.   
I traced the person’s name to a public LinkedIn profile. Then I followed all the references given in his profile and I am still hesitant in offering my private data. The company even has a Linkedin profile of its own, but, wait… the big size of the team involved is 2-10 employees. What happened to the 201–500 people on Wellfound? I went deeper and found the company as a LLC registered in New York - ownership, balance sheets, profit/loss statements, or revenue figures for private LLCs in New York are not publicly available, so there is another question mark red flagging. I could go even deeper, but I lost interest in the subject, and my article is already too long.   
Be careful who you trust with your data. There are plenty of lists on sale on dark-markets. And if you want to invest your money, ask for due diligence first. You might be missing important things.

💡 More on Milburn: Milburn and the demand side 💡 

Suppose DWP and the mayoral strategic authorities get FES right. The service is well designed, commissioned properly, and joined up locally.

That’s still only half the job.

Let’s try a footballing analogy. The best Premier League football academies have great coaches, and talented young players that are ready to step up to the first team. But a football club may hold on to its experienced players, retain a smaller squad (football is a pricey business), and can struggle with the increasing cost of tying young players down to professional contracts.

That’s the jobs market for young people now. Breaking into it is far from straightforward.

Three pressures are coming together.

➕ Falling demand. AI isn’t causing mass layoffs. But it is slowing recruitment. Employers are keeping experienced staff, and not replacing people who leave. Entry-level roles are the easiest to leave unfilled, or to do away with completely.

➕ Rising costs. In real terms, the cost of hiring a young person has risen 48% since 2011-12, from £17,600 to £26,100, with more than half of that rise coming in the last three years.

➕ More regulation. New employment rights make every hire a bigger commitment. That’s hardest to justify when the candidate has no track record.

Against that, a £3,000 hiring grant barely touches the sides of a job costing close to £30,000 a year. And there’s something odd about raising taxes on employment with one hand while subsidising it with the other. Countries with low NEET rates, such as the Netherlands, have far lower minimum wages for young people, compared with typical pay, than we do. We’re not arguing for copying them, but the gap shows where the pressure is.

Most of the policy response is about the supply side - guarantees, advisers, training places. They all matter. But, to return to our footballing analogy, we’re training players that clubs are unable to sign.

Cutting the cost of a first hire needs to come sooner. Otherwise we’ll have built a great academy whose players never get a game.

Great evening at the Melia Hotel for this 𝐖𝐨𝐫𝐤𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐜𝐞 𝐄𝐯𝐨𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐒𝐮𝐦𝐦𝐢𝐭 organized by jobs.lu on the future of work.
 
Julius Probst, PhD kicked things off with the macro picture: growth remains fairly solid, but inflation is picking up again. The job vacancy rate is back to 2019 levels (relatively low) and unemployment has been rising across the Greater Region since 2022, with a "graduate recession" hitting young talent particularly hard. Southern Europe is doing well, but France, Belgium, Luxembourg and Germany now show the lowest vacancy rates.
 
Then Orsolya Kovacs-Ondrejkovic explained how AI is transforming work on three levels: tasks, talents, and teams. She emphasized five key dimensions for HR to mobilize enterprise-wide: Anticipate (map impacted roles and manage career trajectories), Transform (align HR processes with future needs), Build adoption (create trust through ethical frameworks), Drive change and upskill (support day-to-day behavioral shifts), and Lead by example (integrate AI into HR’s own practices). Successful AI adoption is 70% people, organization and process, 20% technology and data, and only 10% algorithms.
 
Finally, Simône van Schouwenburg (Spuerkeess) spoke about attracting and retaining international talent. This resonated with me since I regularly recruit profiles relocating to Luxembourg from abroad: it’s a double challenge. Hiring someone overseas and managing everything around the move (bank account setup, financial uncertainty before the first paycheck, housing, and often family considerations). Her advice: support before arrival (early banking guidance), during onboarding (dedicated contact), and after (regular check-ins). The result? Faster productivity and better retention.
 
My takeaway: whether integrating AI or welcoming international talent, technology and contracts aren’t enough : it’s the human support that makes the difference.
 
A big thank you to jobs.lu, whose teams know how to bring together and consider all the actors of the Luxembourg market.

Imagine a Michelin-starred restaurant.

The head chef knows flavours, ingredients, techniques and what separates an extraordinary dish from an ordinary one. But the restaurant gives someone who has never cooked the responsibility of visiting the market, identifying the finest ingredients, assessing their quality and deciding which ones deserve to enter the kitchen.

The chef gets to see whatever arrives. 
Who designed this operating model? 

Now replace the restaurant with a corporation.

An Engineering Head needs an exceptional engineer.
A Data Director needs an outstanding analyst.
A Sales Head needs a genuine rainmaker.
Yet the responsibility for finding these professionals is frequently handed to HR recruitment.

Why?

Why should the person who understands the profession wait for someone else to discover the professionals? We've created an organisational paradox: the people accountable for business performance are often not accountable for discovering the talent that drives it.

Let's call it what it is: Talent Ownership Deficit.

A radical redesign.

1. PEOPLE MANAGERS: OWN THE HUNT.
Not just the job description. Not just the final interview. The actual sourcing. Identify exceptional professionals in the market. Build relationships before vacancies arise. Participate in professional communities. Recognise capability beyond résumé keywords. Maintain a continuous talent pipeline. Select the people they want in their teams. A manager who cannot identify talent in their own discipline has a management capability gap worth examining.

2. HR: OWN THE EMPLOYMENT ENGINE.
Once the business identifies and selects its candidate for an approved vacancy, HR takes over. Compensation. Offers. Verification. Contracts. Documentation. Onboarding. Compliance. Employee lifecycle. HR becomes the custodian of employment governance, not the default owner of discovering every specialist in the organisation.

3. ACCOUNTABILITY: NO MORE HOT-POTATO MANAGEMENT.
Wrong talent selected? The business manager owns the decision. Poor employment governance? HR owns the failure. No more blaming recruitment for a manager's inability to recognise talent. No more expecting recruiters to possess expertise in every profession they source.

THE QUESTION FOR THE BOARDROOM

Why do we expect managers to own revenue, delivery, innovation, technology and customer satisfaction, but allow them to outsource the responsibility of finding the people who deliver all of these?

Is it genuinely a specialisation problem? Or have we institutionalised Managerial Abdication and rebranded it as recruitment efficiency?

AI can search millions of profiles. ATS platforms can process thousands of applications. Recruitment agencies can supply endless databases. But none of these automatically gives an organisation the ability to recognise exceptional talent. That requires domain understanding. And domain understanding already exists inside the business.

Stop outsourcing talent discovery.

Let managers find the people. Let HR establish and govern the employment relationship. Because the most expensive recruitment failure isn't necessarily hiring the wrong person.
Sometimes, it is never discovering the right person in the first place.

AI agents don’t just answer questions anymore, they act. But who decides what they’re allowed to do?

Picture hiring a house cleaner and handing over a spare key.

Now picture that cleaner also paying your bills and reordering supplies on your behalf, without asking.

That is what agentic AI does, it doesn’t just suggest. It acts, inside your systems, with your data.

This is where many AI deals go wrong. The demo looks great and someone signs. Nobody at the leadership level asks what the AI is allowed to do, who is watching it, or how to stop it.

IBM’s 2026 breach report found that among companies hit by an AI-related breach, 92% lacked proper access controls on their AI systems. The right locks were missing.

The tough part is rarely the technology. It is leaders deciding who owns the AI and changing how the company approves, monitors and measures it. Companies that treat this as a leadership call get the value they paid for.

I had the privilege of attending 116 Pall Mall & Institute of Directors (IoD) for the Better Hiring Institute (BHI) launch of the national hiring index surrounded by dignitaries and industry leaders.

Jonathan Berry, Dido Harding, Lord Nick Markham CBE, Lord Kulveer Ranger, Matthew Taylor, Sarah Olney, Lee Barron MP, Tim Clement-Jones, Lord Kulveer Ranger

It was quite inspiring the way leaders spoke with gravitas, but it was the conversations in-between with my peers that awed me.

Rob Walker FREC BIoR, Keith Rosser, Lili Hunneybel, Steve Betts, Jim B., Duncan Lockett, Greg Wyatt, Lucy Andrews, Danny Caines, Jack Jarrett, Jo Major, Annabel Ashley, Jeremy Thornton, Bill Boorman. 

People have worked really hard to realise these measures. It’s now up to us on the front-line to deliver them.

The real crux of this is getting people into work more quickly into well-fitting roles. The index provides a single comparable view of how hiring is performing across the UK with 9 key metrics.

Out of 150 million UK job applications annually, only 3 million lead to a hire. 1.25 million of those individuals leave within 12 weeks due to poor fit. Broken hiring is costing the UK £75bn a year.

In the UK specifically, employers receive an average of 250 to 280 applications per corporate role. Only 3% of applicants get invited to an initial interview. Tribepad shows applications per job jumped to nearly 49 per vacancy across the wider economy. AI & dehumanisation is a real issue. 

I am currently on the candidate side of that as a TA consultant being unemployed in a tough market, let alone people with less experience or facing additional barriers.

Downtime between contracts means learning time. It’s an investment from my side, ensuring I know my stuff. Time in contracts means application of that knowledge, and I’m fired up and ready to deliver both for candidates and employers.

What does a company who recruits owe a candidate other than the opportunity to apply? 
 
The answer is proportional reciprocity. What you owe scales with what you ask of someone.

I opened my calendar to help people navigating layoffs. I ended up learning a lot myself.

Two days ago, I opened my calendar for 1:1 conversations with people affected by layoffs or struggling to find their next opportunity.

The response completely surprised me.

Here's what happened in the last 48 hours:

- 744 page views and 310 unique visitors on my topmate.io page
- 32 sessions booked
- 33,500+ impressions on that single LinkedIn post
- Nearly 50,000 impressions across the week

More importantly, I spent hours speaking with mobile developers, backend engineers, QA specialists, and ERP architects with 2 to 12+ years of experience.

Different backgrounds. Different experiences. But surprisingly similar challenges.

Here are 4 patterns I noticed:

Applications without responses: Sending 60 to 70+ applications through job portals and barely hearing back.

Lengthy hiring processes: Going through 5 to 6 interview rounds, only to face delayed decisions or no updates.

Changing market expectations: Experienced engineers facing rejections as companies restructure teams, reconsider budgets, and adapt to AI.

Limited visibility: Depending entirely on traditional job portals instead of building a visible professional presence.

Here are some things we explored during these conversations:

1. Alternative earning opportunities

Exploring global AI training and contract platforms where engineers and language experts can find project-based work, with some opportunities offering $10 to $40/hour.

2. Proof of work over resumes

Creating short demo videos of real projects, sharing technical learnings, and demonstrating skills publicly instead of waiting for a resume to get shortlisted.

3. Community over cold applications

Connecting with local tech communities, developer conferences, meetups, and peer networks where meaningful conversations and referrals can happen.

4. Building instead of waiting

Using this transition period to build small products, experiment with AI workflows, and explore freelance consulting.

These are not guaranteed shortcuts to a job. They are additional ways to create opportunities while continuing the job search.

One more honest learning:

Around 10 to 15% of the people who booked a free session didn't show up or even send a message.

I completely understand that circumstances can change. But every unused slot could have gone to someone else who genuinely needed that conversation.

So, going forward, I'm introducing a small ₹149 commitment fee for each 30-minute 1:1 session.

This isn't about monetizing someone's difficult situation. It's simply to reduce no-shows and ensure that every available slot goes to someone who is ready to show up and make the most of our conversation.

If you're navigating a layoff, struggling with your job search, or simply want to brainstorm your next career move, let's connect.

In 2026, the tech industry is losing an average of 1,115 jobs a day - nearly double last year's pace. Meta, Oracle, Block - all citing AI as the reason.

But the most vulnerable group isn't the whole industry. Employment for developers aged 22-25 has fallen nearly 20% from its 2022 peak while employment for developers over 26 has grown. The share of companies actively cutting junior roles jumped from 17% to 43% in a single year.

I read these numbers and found myself thinking about an old story.

In 2019, Bloomberg published an investigation into Boeing. It turned out the company had spent years outsourcing critical 737 Max software development to contract engineers paid as little as $9 an hour - to cut costs. Boeing was laying off experienced engineers and pressuring suppliers to do the same. One manager reportedly said at an all-hands meeting that the company didn't need senior engineers anymore - the products were "mature enough."

It ended in two crashes and 346 deaths.

But what interests me right now isn't the tragedy itself. It's what happened after.

Twenty years. Boeing still hasn't recovered the level of internal engineering expertise it lost back then. Because when you stop growing specialists, you're not just saving money in the moment. You're removing a rung from the ladder that leads to senior-level expertise 10-15 years down the line.

And that's exactly what worries me in the 2026 numbers.

MIT researcher Andrew McAfee asks a simple question: how do people actually learn complex knowledge work, except by practicing on simpler tasks alongside someone who already knows how? When we automate the junior role too quickly, we're not just cutting costs. We're dismantling the apprenticeship ladder that produces tomorrow's senior specialists.

IBM went the other direction - tripling junior hiring specifically because it understands this risk. Most companies are choosing the short-term gain.

I don't know if we'll see a new "Boeing moment" because of AI. But history has already shown what happens when expertise stops being passed to the next generation and the cost of that turns out to be far higher than the money saved.

How do you see this risk in your industry? 👇

I begrudge paying for Sales Navigator. This week I worked out why.
 
Navigator gives you one source of data: LinkedIn. That's it.
 
No emails. No phone numbers. Filters built for a billion users, so they fit nobody. And your lists stay locked inside LinkedIn.
 
So for years I've done what most of us do. Build the list in one tool, check it in Navigator, find contact details in another, research in ten browser tabs, then copy it all into the CRM.
 
Yesterday I had a great catch-up with Dru Carpenter, an AI wizard. Every time we hang out, I realise I'm not pushing AI or my own knowledge far enough. Somewhere between the swim, sauna, steam room and cold plunge, the light bulb went on.
 
With APIs, I can pull all of that into one place.
 
So I built my own list builder, for a client in a niche market.
 
You build a list by picking:
 ↳ who buys: the companies that actually buy from them
 ↳ which buyer: titles mapped to each product they sell
 ↳ where: their regions, not LinkedIn's
 ↳ why now: new in role, company news, new senior hire, hiring, growth
 ↳ the rules: people per company, verified email or mobile only
 ↳ who to leave out: existing customers and open deals
 
Then it gets to work:
 ↳ AI checks every person for fit. Wrong company, gone. Wrong role, gone.
 ↳ An AI agent researches every good-fit company: contract wins, deals, news, with sources
 ↳ It tells you how strong the reason to reach out is
 ↳ It drafts an opener to the right person, based on a real signal
 ↳ Emails and mobiles are revealed only for the people you want
 
It lives in a Google Sheet with a simple app on top. The client can change their ideal customer, buyers, signals and what the AI knows about them right in the sheet. No code.
 
And because it's just APIs, it plugs into what they already use. Their CRM, so existing customers are left out and every contact and brief lands on the record. Tender sites, event lists, direct mail.
 
So nobody opens Navigator. Nobody digs around the CRM to work out who to call. One screen: the person, the reason, the contact details.
 
Built around one business. Change the context and it works for any.
 
First run: 25 people. 10 cut as a poor fit. Every one left came with contact details and a reason to call this week.
 
The important bit: none of this goes into an automated sequence or a LinkedIn drip.
 
It's there so I can do the things only a human can:
 ↳ pick up the phone and have a proper conversation
 ↳ write an email myself, with AI helping, that's actually about them
 ↳ send something physical through the post
 ↳ know which event to be at, and who to find there
 
Navigator's walled garden is LinkedIn's data. Mine is the human stuff: the call, the handwritten note, the handshake.
 
The tools do the research. I do the talking.
 
Paying for Navigator and still building lists across five tabs? Send me your ideal customer in one line. I'll show you what a list built this way looks like for your market.

💔 This is a difficult post to write, but it’s important to be honest about where I’m at right now. A little while ago, I accepted what I believed was a stable, full-time opportunity. After conversations, negotiations, and assurances about the future, I was encouraged to put my own creative work with Napkin Studios aside and focus entirely on the company.

And I did. Because I trusted the people I was working with. I believed in what we discussed and thought I was stepping into something long-term.

Unfortunately, that opportunity was taken away almost as quickly as it came, without warning or time to prepare because of budget constraints.

It’s frustrating. Not just because I lost a job, but because I made decisions about my livelihood based on promises I believed in. When something like that changes overnight, there’s no magical reset button. You still have bills, responsibilities, and a life to maintain.

I am, asking my network for a little help.

I’m looking for work immediately. Full-time would be ideal, but I’m open to contract opportunities as well.

I have 14+ years of experience across product design, mobile/web design, visual design, branding, creative direction, and everything in between. I’ve been fortunate to work on projects for companies like Google and Disney, alongside startups and growing businesses.

I’m not looking for a handout. I’m looking for an opportunity to do what I love, contribute something meaningful, and have a little stability again.

I also want to acknowledge something that’s been weighing on me.

Being a creative right now is hard. With AI transforming our industry at such an incredible pace, navigating an already competitive job market has become even more complicated. We’re expected to constantly adapt, evolve, and prove our value in ways that can honestly feel exhausting.

I know I’m not alone.

I see so many incredibly talented designers, artists, and creatives sharing similar stories. People with years of experience who just want to work, create, and support themselves.

I’m not complaining. I’m not asking for special treatment. I just want a fair opportunity and a little room to breathe.

I’m sharing this because I know how isolating this experience can feel, and because sometimes asking for help is the hardest part.

If you know of anyone hiring, have a referral, need an experienced designer, or could simply share this post with your network, I’d appreciate it more than you know.

You can see my work here:
https://napkin-studios.com 

I also have private case studies available upon request because of NDA.

To all my fellow creatives navigating layoffs, uncertainty, rejection emails, or just trying to figure out what’s next, please hang in there

I genuinely hope nobody has to experience this kind of situation. If you’re going through something similar, I’m rooting for you too. If you need someone to talk to do not hesitate to reach out. ❤️

#Hiring: AI-Powered Web & Mobile App Developer

Organization: A Christian Organization  
Location:Remote  
Work Arrangement:Flexible Hours | Part-Time, Full-Time, or Contract

About the Role

A Christian organization passionate about helping children learn and understand Scripture from an early age is seeking a skilled Web & Mobile App Developer.

This is a flexible, remote, results-driven role with the freedom to manage your own schedule while meeting agreed project milestones and deadlines.

The ideal candidate must be able to leverage AI tools to rapidly transform AI-generated wireframes, designs, and code into secure, scalable, production-ready websites and mobile applications.

Key Responsibilities

- Build and maintain websites and Android/iOS applications using AI-assisted development tools.
- Convert AI-generated prototypes and code into fully functional, production-ready solutions.
- Develop engaging, interactive Scripture-learning applications for children.
- Deploy, publish, secure, troubleshoot, and maintain applications.
- Independently manage projects from concept to launch.

Requirements

Mandatory: Must have successfully launched at least one application currently live and functional on both Android and iOS.
- Proven experience with AI development tools such as Cursor, Claude Code, ChatGPT, or GitHub Copilot.
- Strong full-stack development skills, including frontend, backend, APIs, databases, and security.
- Experience publishing and managing applications on the Apple App Store and Google Play Store.
- Ability to work independently, manage time effectively, and meet deadlines.
- Passion for Christian education and helping children grow in God's Word.

Interview Process
Shortlisted candidates must demonstrate a live application they have built, explain their personal contributions, walk through relevant code and architecture, and discuss their AI development workflow.

How to Apply

Email abidemi@hesedresource.com
Please include the following in your application:
- Resume and portfolio.
- Links to live applications on both the Apple App Store and Google Play Store.
- A brief description of your contributions to the published applications.

Email Subject: Application – AI-Powered Web & Mobile App Developer

NOTE: Applicants with only prototypes or unpublished applications will not be considered.
